extracted.intended_audience: agency decisionmakers, administrative lawyers, judges, and practitioners applying the Administrative Procedure Act
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for agency adjudications, licensing actions, imposition of sanctions, and judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act (sections 8–10). Guidance for what agencies must include in records and decisions and how courts review agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and support for exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to decisions should be precise and supported by specific citations to the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blanket or general exceptions are disfavored; parties should avoid exceptions that merely seek a complete reexamination without reference to pages in the record. Exceptions should focus on meaning, content, and exactness to narrow the issues on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to submit proposed findings, exceptions, and supporting reasons (Section 8(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to each recommended, initial, or tentative decision (or agency review of a subordinate's decision) parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit (1) proposed findings and conclusions, (2) exceptions to decisions or recommended decisions, and (3) supporting reasons for such exceptions or proposed findings or conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure is a codification of general practice; proposed findings are ordinarily submitted to the officers making the initial decision and exceptions thereafter if the result is contested. Exceptions may, in form or effect, include proposed findings or conclusions for the reviewing authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may require precise citation and time limits for submittals
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may require that proposed findings and conclusions and exceptions be supported by precise citation of the record or legal authorities, and may impose reasonable time limits for submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opportunity to submit supporting reasons means briefs on law and facts filed in support of proposed findings/conclusions and exceptions must be received and considered. Section 8(b) does not prescribe opportunities for oral argument; agencies decide when oral argument is necessary or appropriate, subject to other statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record must show ruling on each presented finding, conclusion, or exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The record shall show the ruling upon each such finding, conclusion, or exception presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All decisions (including initial, recommended, or tentative) shall become part of the record and include (1) findings and conclusions, and the reasons or basis therefor, on all material issues of fact, law, or discretion presented on the record; and (2) the appropriate rule, order, sanction, relief, or denial thereof. Purpose: to preclude later controversy as to what the agency had done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings and conclusions must be related to the record and advise parties of their basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that the agency must state the basis for its findings and conclusions means that such findings and conclusions must be sufficiently related to the record as to advise the parties of their record basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements of reasons may be long or short depending on the nature, novelty, or complexity of issues. Agencies typically do so by opinions which reason and relate the issues of fact, law, and discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all relevant issues presented by the record in light of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings and conclusions must include all the relevant issues presented by the record in the light of the law involved; they may be few or many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particular legal conclusion may render certain issues/finding immaterial. Where oral testimony is conflicting or credibility is material, the credibility of witnesses should be a necessary finding. Relevant issues extend to administrative discretion as well as law and fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of basis for exercise or failure to exercise discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions must disclose the basis for the exercise of, or failure to exercise, discretionary power so parties can determine what other facts to offer on rehearing or reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without disclosure of the basis for discretion, parties cannot determine what additional facts might be offered; this requirement codifies existing good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative opinions acceptable if they indicate findings and conclusions with specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency issuing opinions in narrative and expository form need not make separate findings of fact and conclusions of law, but such opinions must indicate findings and conclusions on material issues of fact, law, or discretion with such specificity as to advise the parties and any reviewing court of their record and legal basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative opinions must still communicate the agency's rulings and bases; agencies should ensure sufficient specificity even when not using discrete findings/conclusions headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of agency employees as assistants and conflict limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency heads may utilize agency employees as assistants for analysis and drafting, but in adjudicatory cases subject to section 5(c) such assistants could not have performed investigative or prosecuting functions in the cases (or factually related cases) in which they are so employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing officers who heard a case may draft final decisions and otherwise assist in formulation, but investigators/prosecutors in the same matter should not perform those drafting roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals to superior agency preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in section 8 is intended to cut off rights parties may have for appeal to or review by a superior agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form/content requirements of subsection 8(b) do not apply to decisions of a superior agency upon appeal or review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions must be within delegated jurisdiction and authorized by law (Section 9(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: In the exercise of any power or authority no sanction shall be imposed or substantive rule or order be issued except within jurisdiction delegated to the agency and as authorized by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'sanction' is broadly defined to include prohibitions, withholding of relief, penalties, seizure of property, assessment of damages/costs/fees, revocation/suspension of licenses, and other compulsory or restrictive actions. Authority may derive from statutes, treaties, court decisions, commonly recognized administrative practices, or other law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must not appropriate powers Congress did not intend
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of section 9(a) is to assure agencies will not appropriate to themselves powers Congress has not intended them to exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency powers may be express or implied; whether express or implied, powers must be exercised within authority. Congress left adaptation of means to ends to administrative processes, but agencies must act within authorized bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing proceedings must be completed with reasonable dispatch (Section 9(b) — applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application is made for a license required by law the agency, with due regard to rights of interested parties and with reasonable dispatch, shall set and complete any proceedings required and make its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Reasonable dispatch' is not precise and varies by agency and type of license; where another statute prescribes a specific period, that controls. If statute requires record after hearing, sections 7 and 8 procedures apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension/revocation of licenses requires notice and opportunity to comply except in willfulness or public safety cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in cases of willfulness or those in which public health, interest, or safety requires otherwise, no withdrawal, suspension, revocation, or annulment of any license shall be lawful unless, prior to proceedings, facts or conduct which may warrant such action have been called to the licensee in writing and the licensee afforded opportunity to demonstrate or achieve compliance with lawful requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The warning must be in writing but need not take special form. No prior notice required if conduct is willful or immediate action required for public safety. Provisions do not apply to temporary permits/licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary permits and renewals treated differently re notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice/opportunity requirement does not apply to temporary permits or temporary licenses; such permits may be revoked without 'another chance.' The renewal situation is addressed separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may revoke temporary licenses immediately regardless of willfulness or public health considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal protection when timely and sufficient application filed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the licensee has, in accordance with agency rules, made timely and sufficient application for renewal or a new license, no license for continuing activity shall expire until such application has been finally determined by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may make reasonable rules requiring sufficient advance application. This protects licensees who have done everything required from suffering lapse due to agency delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review — general restatement (Section 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 restates principles of judicial review: agency action is subject to judicial review except so far as (1) statutes preclude judicial review or (2) agency action is by law committed to agency discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 10 deals largely with principles and must be coordinated with special statutory review provisions. It does not supersede special statutory review proceedings and leaves mechanics to statutes and judicial rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutes may preclude or limit judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: A statute may expressly preclude judicial review, or courts may interpret a statute as intended to preclude review; where Congress intends to preclude review, section 10's provisions do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include statutes declaring particular administrative decisions 'final and conclusive.' Courts may also deduce that review is precluded from statutory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency action committed to discretion may be unreviewable
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency action that is by law committed to agency discretion (e.g., actions 'if in his judgment') may be unreviewable under section 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many loan-authorizing statutes give agencies discretion so complete that refusal to make a loan is not reviewable. Refusal by NLRB to issue a complaint is another example of unreviewable discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons entitled to judicial review (Section 10(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person suffering legal wrong because of any agency action, or adversely affected or aggrieved by such action within the meaning of any relevant statute, shall be entitled to judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'legal wrong' is used as a limitation and not to make review available to anyone merely adversely affected. 'Adversely affected or aggrieved' is determined by courts following existing doctrine and statutory interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of proceeding and venue for judicial review (Section 10(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of proceeding for judicial review shall be any special statutory review proceeding relevant to the subject matter in any court specified by statute or, absent/ inadequate statutory procedure, any applicable form of legal action (declaratory judgments, injunctions, habeas corpus) in any court of competent jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where special statutory review proceedings exist they will continue; in their absence or inadequacy, courts will select appropriate forms. The Act leaves 'adequacy' to the courts' determination and does not define it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue unchanged by section 10(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10(b) does not alter existing venue requirements for judicial review; review remains in courts specified by statute or courts of competent jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes that specify a particular court (e.g., D.C. Circuit for FCC orders) remain controlling. General venue statutes (e.g., 28 U.S.C. 112) continue to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review in enforcement proceedings and prior adequate/exclusive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency action shall be subject to judicial review in civil or criminal proceedings for judicial enforcement except to the extent that prior, adequate, and exclusive opportunity for such review is provided by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision preserves the present rule: where Congress has provided an exclusive prior method of review that is adequate, enforcement proceedings may not be a vehicle for collateral attack. The doctrine of primary jurisdiction and exhaustion of administrative remedies is preserved.
